classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange the equations, rewrite the harder discriminant as a sum of squares to prove positivity, and handle the linear and identity cases separately.

content.prompt: Prove that the roots of the following equations are always real.

answer.short: Real roots, since $\Delta=p^2+4q^2\ge0$ in the quadratic case. When $p=0$, the equation has $x=\frac12$ if $q\ne0$, or every real $x$ if $q=0$.
answer.worked:
For $p\ne0$, write $px^2-(p+2q)x+q=0$.

$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(p+2q)^2-4pq\\\Delta&=p^2+4q^2\\\Delta&>0\end{align*}$$

So the quadratic has two distinct real roots. If $p=0$ and $q\ne0$, then $q=2qx$ gives $x=\frac12$. If $p=q=0$, every real $x$ satisfies the equation.

answer.short: Real roots, since $\Delta=(p-q)^2+4q^2\ge0$ in the quadratic case. When $q=0$, the equation has $x=-1$ if $p\ne0$, or every real $x$ if $p=0$.
answer.worked:
For $q\ne0$, expand and rearrange to give $qx^2+(p+q)x+(p-q)=0$.

$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(p+q)^2-4q(p-q)\\\Delta&=p^2-2pq+5q^2\\\Delta&=(p-q)^2+4q^2\\\Delta&>0\end{align*}$$

So the quadratic has two distinct real roots. If $q=0$ and $p\ne0$, then $p(1+x)=0$ gives $x=-1$. If $p=q=0$, every real $x$ satisfies the equation.
